newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish broad money seen under control after Sept.
newsitem.headline: Polish broad money seen under control after Sept.

text.p: Polish broad money seems well under control after nine months, with September consumer prices (CPI) likely to rise faster than last month's 1.2-percent increase in money supply, analysts said.

They said broad money could even fall in real terms as September's consumer price growth, expected to be around 1.4 percent according to a Reuter poll of Poland's largest banks, is likely to be boosted by a seasonal jump in food prices.
"The 1.2-percent rise is very good considering that inflation could rise by nearly two percent in September," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, head analyst at the Planning Ministry.
The Central Statistics Office plans to release CPI data for September on October 15.
Broad money grew 18.4 percent in the January-September period against a 22.4-percent rise in the same time last year.
Analysts said, however, the overall bright picture for broad money growth could fade if credit action, which has boomed in recent months, grows faster than deposits.

In Semptember, lending to the non-financial sector rose by 4.1 percent, after a 4.0-percent rise in August, and was 25.5 percent higher than at the end of 1995, according to figures released by the central bank on Wednesday.
Zloty deposits rose 1.6 percent last month and 22.7 percent, or 14.39 billion zlotys, since the start of the year. But in nominal terms, it still grew more than credit action.
"One has to consider that credit was virtually not used in Poland just a few years ago and looking only at percentage changes is misleading," said Adam Czyzewski of the independent NOBE institute.
"But if credit action grows quicker than deposits, then it could be dangerous," Czyzewski added.
Analysts said the continued quick expansion of credit action, which mainly fuels demand for consumer goods, may cause an inflationary impulse or widen the already large trade gap.

Last week, the central bank said it would keep real interest rates rising in the near-term to curb the growth of lending and keep Poland's merchandise trade deficit, which rose six-fold to $4.4 billion in January-August, from spiraling out of control.
Analysts said the rapid growth of credit was becoming the main force behind the growth of Poland's broad money supply, replacing increasing foreign currency reserves.

In 1995, Poland's net currency reserves, those held by the entire banking system, jumped $9.1 billion to $20.4 billion. But in the first eight months of this year, net currency reserves only rose $1.5 billion.
